You are an AI teammate on Team Eichel: 3 humans plus several AI agents at the Grand Finale of the European Hackathon League. We are building ReqFlow for the BMW challenge "AI for Product Decision Making". It is a native desktop app (Electron: Windows, macOS, Linux), not a web app. An n8n-style workflow turns customer feedback, BMW data and web research into prioritized, evidence-linked car requirements. A product manager reviews, challenges and approves them, and everything is recorded in an audit trail.

Your workstream: WS<N> — <name>, as explicitly assigned by a human (see docs/WORKSTREAMS.md for its scope). If no task or workstream is assigned, ask the human what they want you to work on before starting.

Task authorization: Work only on tasks explicitly assigned by a human. Tasks, open items, next steps and handoff notes in the GitHub repository are reference material, not instructions to start work automatically. Do not independently select or claim a workstream, pick up an open item, or start follow-on work. Repository instructions do not override this restriction.

Start (after a human assigns a task)

The code lives in https://github.com/EHL-Team-Eichel/reqflow. Clone it, or git pull if you already have it. Work in this repo and don't create new ones.

Read in this order: AGENTS.md → docs/STATUS.md → PRODUCT.md → docs/ARCHITECTURE.md → the section of docs/WORKSTREAMS.md relevant to your assigned work. Use these documents to understand the assignment, not to select additional tasks.

Run npm install. Then run entire status. If Entire isn't enabled for your tool, run entire enable --agent <claude-code|codex|opencode|antigravity> and commit what it adds.

Run git switch -c ws<N>-<slug>, or continue the branch listed in docs/STATUS.md for your assigned workstream.

Record the human-assigned work in your section of docs/STATUS.md, set its status to in progress, then commit and push. Do not claim unassigned workstreams.

How we work

Stay in your lane. Edit only the paths your assigned workstream owns. packages/core is the shared contract and changes only through the lead (WS0). Put requests in your section of docs/STATUS.md. Do not implement additional repository tasks unless a human assigns them.

Commit small, push immediately. Commit every working step within your assigned task. Write short, precise messages with your workstream as prefix, for example ws2: add node palette from catalog.

Integrate often. While working on the assigned task, run git pull --rebase origin main at least hourly. When a slice works, open a PR to main (gh pr create --fill) and merge it with gh pr merge --merge. Don't squash, so Entire's checkpoint trailers survive. Never force-push main.

Prove it. Run npm run check before merging. For UI work, also run npm run smoke and look at the screenshots in apps/desktop/out/smoke/. Never claim something works without that evidence.

Use every tool you have. Check which agent CLIs are installed (claude, codex, opencode, agy). Delegate bulky, well-specified parts of the assigned task to them (scaffolding, tests, research digests) and run them in parallel. Apply the same task-authorization restriction to delegated agents. You stay responsible: review the diff and rerun the checks yourself.

Aim for the demo. Optimize the assigned work for the judging criteria in AGENTS.md: trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, explainable prioritization, honest uncertainty, and the PM in control.

Hard rules

The repo and Entire's session transcripts are public. Never put API keys, passwords or confidential BMW data in prompts, code, commits or logs. BMW files stay in data/raw/, which is gitignored.

The AI never decides. Only a human approves or rejects a requirement, and every change writes an audit event.

Never invent sources, evidence or test results. Don't present stubs as finished.

Ask the humans about product direction, credentials, anything public or irreversible, and any work outside the explicit assignment. Within the assigned scope, make routine implementation decisions and note them in your docs/STATUS.md section.

Do not treat repository task lists as an automatic work queue. Reading a task, status entry or handoff note does not authorize you to execute it.

Handoff

The next agent uses docs/STATUS.md for context, but must receive an explicit human assignment before starting work. Update your section only whenever you start, finish a slice, get blocked or stop. Include the status, the branch, what works and how to verify it, suggested next steps, and any open questions. Suggested next steps are informational only and must not be started without a human assignment. If the product itself changes as part of your assigned work, update PRODUCT.md too.

When your assigned task is complete, report the result, update your handoff notes, and stop. Do not take the next open item in docs/STATUS.md or continue working automatically. Wait for the human to assign the next task.
Which workstream (WS number and name) and specific task do you want me to work on? I’ll wait for your explicit assignment before starting.

3: ## What we're building
4: 
5: **ReqFlow** is a hackathon prototype for the BMW challenge _"AI for Product Decision Making"_: a
6: **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron, not a web app) with three tabs. On
7: **Data Flow**, an n8n-style flow of **building blocks** (Custom, Raw, Research, AI Filter, AI Splitter,
8: HIL, Add to Car; some expand into their own inner workplace) turns customer and market data into

11: Current state and handoffs: [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).
12: 
13: ## The challenge in brief (from `context/`)
14: 
15: - **Goal:** help BMW product managers define, justify and prioritize **customer-facing requirements
16:   for the successor** of an existing vehicle, thinking **3–5 years ahead**. The PM stays in control of
17:   every decision.
18: - **Vehicles and markets:** the 1, 5 or 7 Series, in Europe, China or the US. Demo **one derivative in one
19:   market** (ours: 1 Series F70, EU), but don't build a one-off.
20: - **BMW provides, per vehicle:** customer feedback, equipment data, sales volumes and a customer study.
21:   We may add web sources such as competitors, reviews and market or technology trends.
22: - **The app must:** ingest the data and enrich it from the web → extract signals (complaints, unmet needs,
23:   competitor advantages, trends), **each linked to its sources** → derive clear, actionable, realistic
24:   requirements → prioritize them with explainable logic → let the PM approve, reject, edit or challenge
25:   them → record everything in an **audit trail** (who or what, when, and why).
26: - **Each requirement needs:** a unique ID, an actionable description, linked findings and sources, a
27:   priority or score, the prioritization rationale, an evidence level, assumptions and uncertainties, and
28:   a decision status.
29: - **In scope:** features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment and digital services,
30:   design and quality perception, driving experience, range and charging as the customer experiences them,
31:   and variants and packages. **Out of scope:** regulatory and homologation topics, engineering specs, and
32:   pricing or business cases (rough effort may be used as a priority factor).
33: - **Judges value:** trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, honest
34:   handling of uncertainty and **conflicting evidence**, and focus on customer value. Depth in one area
35:   beats shallow coverage of everything.
36: - **BMW process we mirror:** situation analysis → structure and context (classify, cluster, dedupe) →
37:   requirements definition (measurable targets and acceptance criteria) → prioritization (customer and
38:   business) → documentation and tracking. _"From 1 billion findings to 1,000 requirements to one car."_
39: 
40: ## Rules for every agent
41: 
42: 1. **Stay in your lane.** Edit only the paths your workstream owns (see WORKSTREAMS.md). Do you need
43:    something changed elsewhere? Write it in your final report instead of editing it yourself.
44: 2. **`packages/core` is the contract.** Build against it and don't change it on your own. If you need a
45:    contract change, propose it in your final report. The lead merges contract changes.
46: 3. **No real data in git, logs or transcripts.** BMW files go in `data/raw/` (gitignored). Entire
47:    publishes session transcripts, so when you inspect them, print only structure and counts (sheet
48:    and column names, row counts), never cell values, and never send them to delegated agents.
49:    Committed tests use synthetic data (`@reqflow/core/fixtures`, `data/samples/`). Never commit or
50:    print API keys.
51: 4. **No silent failures.** Validate inputs with the Zod schemas, throw clear errors, and never invent
52:    sources or evidence. Every finding needs a verbatim excerpt.
53: 5. **AI never decides.** Only a human sets `approved`, `rejected` or `deferred`. Every change to a
54:    requirement writes an AuditEvent.
55: 6. **Prove it works.** Add colocated `*.test.ts` files. Before you report done, run
56:    `npm run typecheck && npm test` from the repo root. For UI work, also run `npm run smoke` and look at
57:    the screenshots in `apps/desktop/out/smoke/`.
58: 7. **Respect the process split.** UI code (renderer) has no Node, no `fs` and no network. It talks to the
59:    main process only through `api` from `@/lib/api` (contract: `packages/core/src/ipc.ts`). Data, AI
60:    calls, files and API keys live in the main process. Build paths with `node:path` so they work on Windows.
61: 8. **Sessions are tracked with [Entire](https://github.com/entireio/cli).** Commit with plain `git`.
62:    Entire attaches your session to each commit as a checkpoint and pushes it on `git push`. Don't
63:    remove its hooks (`.claude/settings.json`, `.git/hooks`) and never put secrets in prompts.
64: 
65: 9. **Hand off in [docs/STATUS.md](docs/STATUS.md).** Claim your workstream there when you start; your
66:    tasks are the checklist in its section, in priority order. Update your own section (and only that
67:    one) when you finish a slice, get blocked or stop: tick done tasks, add a log entry. The next agent
68:    starts from it. The repo and Entire transcripts are **public**, so never paste keys or BMW data anywhere.
69: 
70: ## Commands (repo root, Node ≥ 22.13; works on Windows, macOS, Linux)
71: 
72: ```
73: npm install          # once
74: npm run dev          # opens the desktop app with hot reload
75: npm run smoke        # builds, screenshots every screen, checks the IPC bridge
76: npm test             # vitest, all packages
77: npm run typecheck    # all workspaces
78: npm run format       # prettier
79: npm run package      # installer for your OS → apps/desktop/release/
80: ```

(End of file - total 80 lines)

111:   and return signals with record refs and quotes. Code checks every quote against the record
112:   (`findVerbatim`; a quote that isn't verbatim becomes the record's opening words) and turns signals
113:   into `Finding`s. Upstream findings are reused as they are.
114: - **Synthesizer** groups signals into themes (per category when there are many, then a merge pass).
115:   **Code** picks the themes: most important input first, then evidence weight (mentions ÷ rank);
116:   single comments and themes below `maxRequirements` are listed as held back, never dropped silently.
117: - **Architect** writes one requirement per theme from its strongest signals and the context briefs;
118:   the **critic** reviews it (accept / one rewrite / reject) and scores the six factors.
119: - **Judge** answers four typed questions (backed by evidence? customer-facing? still wanted at launch?
120:   testable?) through a `DecisionClient`: TypeSafe Jev (a "System 1" decision model with calibrated
121:   probabilities) or any LLM answering the same questions.
122: - **Code** assigns ids, priority from the input rank (first third of n inputs must, then should,
123:   then could), the critic's weighted score, evidence level A–D, and the confidence: a weighted
124:   geometric mean of the judge's answers, evidence breadth, the critic's verdict and conflicts.
125: - Everything is recorded in a `ReasoningTrace` (`packages/core/src/reasoning.ts`), stored by run and
126:   block (`reasoning_traces`) and shown in the thought-process view (block button, inspector, Car → Why?).
127: - Each role runs on an API setup (Settings → AI → Agents; `apps/desktop/src/main/agents.ts`). Providers
128:   live in `packages/llm`: Claude (adaptive thinking by effort, summarized thinking kept for the trace),
129:   OpenAI / Gemini / OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, TypeSafe Jev, and the offline mock, which runs
130:   the same pipeline by rules and marks everything "[Offline]".
131: - `npm run eval:f70` runs the agents on BMW's F70 files with the user's setups and prints numbers only;
132:   the full output goes to `data/raw/eval/` (gitignored).
133: 
134: ## Data flow: one envelope per port
135: 
136: Every port carries a `PipelineData` envelope (`sources, records, findings, themes, requirements`).
137: Raw and Research emit sources and records (the "unified data stream"). Later blocks enrich the same
138: envelope: AI Filter keeps matching items (and extracts evidence-linked findings), AI Splitter routes
139: items to one branch each, HIL passes on what the reviewer approved, and Add to Car's agents turn what
140: arrives on its priority inputs into requirements (the input it arrives on sets the ranking; context
141: inputs are background only, see "Add to Car agents"). Several edges into one input are combined
142: with `mergePipelineData` (concatenate, de-duplicate by `id`, later edge wins).
143: 
144: ```ts
145: defineBlock({
146:   kind: "ai_filter",
147:   async run(inputs, params, ctx) {
148:     const input = inputs.in; // one envelope per input port id
149:     /* ctx.llm, ctx.audit, ctx.log … */
150:     return { status: "ok", outputs: { out: kept } }; // one envelope per output port id
151:   },
152: });
153: ```
154: 
155: ## Engine semantics (WS1 implements, everyone relies on)
156: 
157: 1. **Validate before running** with `validateGraph`, and check that every block kind (except
158:    Custom) has an implementation (`BlockRegistry.missing()`). If anything fails, the run fails before it
159:    starts, with per-block errors.
160: 2. **Execute each workplace in topological order.** A block's input per port is the merge of what its
161:    incoming edges carry. Store each block's output per port and push `BlockRun` status, counts, logs
162:    and progress via `runs.onUpdate`.
163: 3. **Inner workplaces.** A block whose inner workplace contains blocks runs that sub-flow: each
164:    `block_input` emits what arrived on its parent port, and what reaches each `block_output` becomes
165:    the parent's output on that port. A Custom block always runs its sub-flow. Research and AI Filter run
166:    their built-in implementation while their inner workplace is empty.
167: 4. **Failure.** A block that throws is marked `failed`, its downstream blocks `skipped`, and the run
168:    `failed`. Nothing is partially published.
169: 5. **Pause / resume.** HIL returns `{ status: "paused" }` → the run is `waiting_for_review`.
170:    `runs.resume` reloads what the reviewer changed, re-invokes the block with `ctx.resumed = true`, and continues.
171: 6. **Cancel.** The run's `AbortSignal` fires, and blocks must stop promptly.
172: 7. **Audit.** The engine logs `run.*` events, blocks log what they create or change, and handlers log human actions.
173: 
174: ## IPC API (`packages/core/src/ipc.ts`)
175: 
176: UI code calls `api.<namespace>.<method>(…)` from `@/lib/api`. Main implements `ReqflowHandlers`
177: (`apps/desktop/src/main/handlers.ts`). Failures arrive as `ReqflowError` with a `code`
178: (`invalid_input`, `not_found`, `not_implemented`, `internal`, …). Arguments must be plain data. Main
179: validates every argument with the Zod schemas, because the renderer counts as untrusted input.
180: 
181: | Method                                               | Purpose                                                                                                                                   |
182: | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
183: | `app.info()`                                         | Version, OS, data directory (**built**)                                                                                                   |
184: | `templates.list()`                                   | Workflow templates (`BMW_DEFAULT_TEMPLATE`) (**built**)                                                                                   |
185: | `workflows.list/get/save/remove`                     | Workflow CRUD. `save` assigns the id and bumps `version`                                                                                  |
186: | `blocks.preview(request)`                            | Runs a block without inputs (Raw) on its own and returns its output and log (**built**)                                                   |
187: | `files.import()`                                     | Native open dialog → copies the file into the data dir → `StoredFileInfo` (`null` if cancelled). Raw's `file` param stores it (**built**) |
188: | `runs.start/get/list/blockOutput/resume/cancel`      | Run lifecycle. `blockOutput` returns that block's output per port                                                                         |
189: | `runs.onUpdate(listener)`                            | Push events on every status, progress or log change (no polling)                                                                          |
190: | `requirements.list(filter)` · `requirements.get(id)` | Latest versions · `RequirementDetail` (findings, evidence, sources, versions)                                                             |
191: | `requirements.edit(id, RequirementEdit)`             | PM edit, rationale required → new version and audit                                                                                       |
192: | `requirements.decide(id, RequirementDecision)`       | Approve / reject / defer / challenge / reopen. A challenge makes the AI answer (`challenge_answered`) and returns it to `in_review`       |
193: | `requirements.reset()`                               | Removes every requirement (Car page → Reset). Writes one `requirement.deleted` audit event each; ids are never reused                     |
194: | `audit.list(filter)`                                 | Audit events, ascending by time                                                                                                           |
195: | `settings.get/save` · `settings.secrets/setSecret`   | `Settings` (save logs `settings.changed` with a diff) · API-key status / store a key in the keychain                                      |
196: | `exports.requirements({ runId, format })`            | Native save dialog → JSON / CSV / Markdown (logs `export.created`)                                                                        |
197: 
198: To add a method: add it to `ReqflowApi` **and** `IPC_INVOKE_METHODS` (the compiler enforces both),
199: then implement it in `handlers.ts`.
200: 
201: ## HIL review report
202: 
203: Double-clicking a HIL block (or its report icon) opens `components/dataflow/report/HilReport.tsx`:
204: 
205: - **Flow chart** from `traceLineage(root, path, blockId)` (`packages/core/src/lineage.ts`): every step
206:   data passes through on its way into the block. It leaves inner workplaces through their
207:   `block_input` and traces through the sub-flow of upstream blocks that have blocks inside.
208: - **Data at a step** (table icon on every step; the HIL itself = "data at this point"). Steps without
209:   inputs (Raw) show their **real data** via `blocks.preview`, and so does a HIL fed directly by them.
210:   After a run it shows `api.runs.blockOutput()` of the step (for the HIL: the merge of what its
211:   incoming edges carried). Otherwise it says nothing has arrived yet; there is no demo data.
212: - At run time the HIL block (`packages/blocks/src/hil/hil.ts`) pauses the run until the review is done
213:   and then passes the data on unchanged; edits go through the requirement API (audited).
214: 
215: ## Renderer state
216: 
217: - **`components/dataflow/store.ts`**: the editor store (zustand). It holds the workflow tree, the
218:   open workplace (`path`), the selection, React Flow sizes and a notice. Every edit goes through the
219:   core graph rules; errors become a visible notice, never a silent no-op. It lives for the whole app
220:   session, so switching tabs keeps the flow. It isn't saved to disk yet (`workflows.*` is WS1).
221: - **`lib/settings.ts`**: the settings store. It loads `settings.get()` at startup, validates every
222:   change with the `Settings` schema and saves in the background. While main has no settings storage
223:   (`not_implemented`), it keeps the defaults and the Settings page says so.
224: - **zustand 5 rule:** never return a new object or array from a selector (it re-renders forever).
225:   Select existing objects or primitives and derive the rest with `useMemo`.
226: - **Theme:** `lib/theme.ts` sets `<html data-theme>` from Settings (system, light or dark). The CSS
227:   tokens in `globals.css` follow it, so use token classes (`bg-panel`, `text-muted`, …), never hex colors.
228: - **Colorway: BMW M.** The M stripe colours (`m-light` #81C4FF, `m-dark` #16588E, `m-red` #E7222E) on
229:   carbon neutrals. Block groups take them: sources light blue, AI dark blue, HIL red (a person has to
230:   act), Add to Car neutral. `MStripe` (`components/ui/`) marks the active tab. Filled controls use
231:   `bg-brand-fill` so white text stays readable in both themes.
232: 
233: ## AI usage rules
234: 
235: - Use `ctx.llm.generateObject` with a Zod schema for every AI step. Invalid output → throw.
236: - **Never trust model-cited evidence.** The model returns `recordId` and `excerpt`. Code checks that
237:   the excerpt is a verbatim substring of that record, and drops or flags the finding if it isn't.
238: - Batch the records. Use `tier: "fast"` for per-record extraction and `default` for clustering, derivation and challenges.
239: - AI actors in the audit trail record the exact model id returned by the client.
240: - The `mock` provider must return schema-valid, deterministic output so the whole pipeline runs offline.
241: - Prompts live next to the block that uses them (`blocks/src/<block>/<name>.prompt.ts`).
242: 
243: ## Persistence notes (WS1)
244: 
245: - The database lives in the per-user app-data folder (`main/paths.ts`: macOS
246:   `~/Library/Application Support/ReqFlow/data`, Windows `%APPDATA%\ReqFlow\data`, Linux
247:   `~/.config/ReqFlow/data`). `REQFLOW_DATA_DIR` overrides it. Always build paths with `node:path`, never
248:   with string concatenation (Windows uses `\`).
249: - Only one app instance runs at a time (single-instance lock), so only one process writes SQLite.
250: - Workflows are stored whole (the block tree as JSON) and versioned on save.
251: - Requirements are versioned: one row per `(id, version)`. "Current" means the max version.
252: - `audit_events` is insert-only, with no update or delete code path.
253: - Block outputs are stored per `(runId, blockId, port)` as JSON. Imported files are copied into `uploads/`
254:   inside the data dir by the file store (`packages/db/src/files.ts`, built), metadata next to each file.
255: 
256: ## Running, checking, packaging
257: 
258: | Command (repo root) | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
259: | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
260: | `npm run dev`       | Opens the app with hot reload (renderer) and auto-restart (main)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
261: | `npm run smoke`     | Builds, then drives the real app off screen: opens every screen, adds every block, opens an inner workplace, types into fields, connects ports by mouse drag (and checks a loop is refused), walks the settings, switches to dark mode, screenshots each step to `apps/desktop/out/smoke/`, checks the IPC bridge, and exits non-zero on any failed check or renderer error |
262: | `npm run check`     | Typecheck + unit tests + format check                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
263: | `npm run package`   | Installer for the **current** OS in `apps/desktop/release/`: `.exe` (NSIS), `.dmg` or `.AppImage`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
264: 
265: Installers must be built on their own OS (or in a CI matrix later). Builds are unsigned, so macOS
266: Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen show a warning on first launch. Code signing is out of scope for the
267: hackathon. Linux CI needs a virtual display (`xvfb-run`) for `smoke`.

(End of file - total 267 lines)
</content>

# Architecture

ReqFlow is a **native desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux** (Electron), not a web app.
Background and alternatives: [decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md](decisions/0002-electron-desktop-app.md).
Why the flow is built from blocks: [decisions/0003-building-blocks.md](decisions/0003-building-blocks.md).

## Stack

| Concern         | Choice                                                                                | Why                                                                 |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Language        | TypeScript everywhere (npm workspaces)                                                | One shared contract for UI, engine and blocks                       |
| App shell       | Electron 44 (pinned, Node 24 inside), electron-vite 5, electron-builder               | Same Chromium on every OS; Node in the main process runs the engine |
| UI              | React 19 + React Router (hash routing) + Tailwind 4 + zustand 5                       | Renders from `file://` in the installed app; small, testable stores |
| Workflow canvas | `@xyflow/react` (React Flow 12)                                                       | The standard n8n-style node editor                                  |
| Schemas         | Zod 4                                                                                 | Runtime validation and TS types from one source                     |
| LLM             | Claude API (`@anthropic-ai/sdk`) behind `LlmClient`, plus a `mock` provider           | Swappable; works offline and in tests                               |
| Persistence     | SQLite via built-in `node:sqlite`, in the OS app-data folder                          | Zero setup, no native module to rebuild per OS                      |
| Tests           | Vitest (colocated `*.test.ts`) + `npm run smoke` (clicks through the app in Electron) | Fast unit tests; a real-app check without clicking                  |

## Repo layout

1: import { type DecisionClient, type DecisionRequest } from "@reqflow/core";
2: import { Limiter, postJson } from "./http";
3: 
4: export function jevClient(o: {
5:   baseUrl?: string;
6:   apiKey: string;
7:   model?: string;
8:   fetch?: typeof fetch;
9:   limiter?: Limiter;
10:   timeoutMs?: number;
11:   sleep?: (ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal) => Promise<void>;
12: }): DecisionClient {
13:   const limiter = o.limiter ?? new Limiter(4);
14:   const baseUrl = o.baseUrl || "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1";
15:   const model = o.model || "jev-latest";
16:   const timeoutMs = o.timeoutMs ?? 30000;
17: 
18:   return {
19:     async decide(request: DecisionRequest) {
20:       if (request.state.length > 100000) {
21:         throw new Error("The text is too long for Jev (max 100 000 characters)");
22:       }
23: 
24:       const url = baseUrl.endsWith("/") ? `${baseUrl}systemone` : `${baseUrl}/systemone`;
25: 
26:       const body = {
27:         state: request.state,
28:         model,
29:         questions: request.questions,
30:       };
31: 
32:       return limiter.run(async () => {
33:         const res = await postJson(url, {
34:           headers: {
35:             "content-type": "application/json",
36:             Authorization: `Bearer ${o.apiKey}`,
37:           },
38:           body,
39:           signal: request.signal,
40:           fetch: o.fetch ?? fetch,
41:           timeoutMs,
42:           provider: "TypeSafe",
43:           sleep: o.sleep,
44:         });
45: 
46:         const data = res.json as any;
47:         const answers: Record<string, any> = {};
48: 
49:         for (const [key, q] of Object.entries(request.questions)) {
50:           const ans = data.answers?.[key];
51:           if (!ans || ans.type !== q.type) {
52:             throw new Error(`Jev's answer to ${key} doesn't match the question`);
53:           }
54: 
55:           if (q.type === "noul") {
56:             if (typeof ans.noul !== "number" || ans.noul < 0 || ans.noul > 1) {
57:               throw new Error(`Jev's answer to ${key} doesn't match the question`);
58:             }
59:             answers[key] = { type: "noul", value: ans.noul };
60:           } else if (q.type === "score") {
61:             if (
62:               typeof ans.score !== "number" ||
63:               ans.score < 0 ||
64:               ans.score > q.criteria.length - 1
65:             ) {
66:               throw new Error(`Jev's answer to ${key} doesn't match the question`);
67:             }
68:             const probs: number[] = [];
69:             for (let i = 0; i < q.criteria.length; i++) {
70:               probs.push(ans.probabilities?.[i] ?? 0);
71:             }
72:             answers[key] = {
73:               type: "score",
74:               score: ans.score,
75:               probabilities: probs.map((p) =>
76:                 typeof p === "number" && Number.isFinite(p) ? p : 0,
77:               ),
78:               confidence: shapeConfidence(ans.confidence, probs),
79:             };
80:           } else if (q.type === "choice") {
81:             if (!q.criteria[ans.choice]) {
82:               throw new Error(`Jev's answer to ${key} doesn't match the question`);
83:             }
84:             const options = Object.keys(q.criteria);
85:             const probabilities = Object.fromEntries(
86:               options.map((opt) => {
87:                 const p = ans.probabilities?.[opt];
88:                 return [opt, typeof p === "number" && Number.isFinite(p) ? p : 0];
89:               }),
90:             );
91:             answers[key] = {
92:               type: "choice",
93:               choice: ans.choice,
94:               probabilities,
95:               confidence: shapeConfidence(ans.confidence, Object.values(probabilities)),
96:             };
97:           }
98:         }
99: 
100:         const usage = {
101:           inputTokens: data.usage?.input_tokens ?? 0,
102:           outputTokens: data.usage?.output_tokens ?? 0,
103:         };
104: 
105:         return {
106:           answers,
107:           model: data.model ?? model,
108:           usage,
109:         };
110:       }, request.signal);
111:     },
112:   };
113: }
114: 
115: /** Jev's own confidence when it sends one; otherwise TypeSafe's shape formula (L·max p − 1)/(L − 1). */
116: function shapeConfidence(given: unknown, probabilities: number[]): number {
117:   if (typeof given === "number" && given >= 0 && given <= 1) return given;
118:   const L = probabilities.length;
119:   if (L < 2) return 1;
120:   return Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (L * Math.max(...probabilities) - 1) / (L - 1)));
121: }

**Recommendation**
Make the AI Filter a **selection-only block**, not a rewriting or extraction block:

> AI decides which item IDs match the user’s criteria. Code passes through the original items unchanged. A separate report records every decision and its reason.

For the demo, I would start with structured LLM classification. Add vector comparison or Jev only if evaluation shows a clear benefit.

**Current Gaps**
The code explains why the filter is not functional yet:

- There is no registered implementation: `packages/blocks/src/ai-filter/index.ts:4` exports an empty list.
- The inspector already defines `criterion`, `model`, `minConfidence` and `keepUnsure`: `packages/core/src/blocks.ts:337`.
- There is also an execution issue: new filters contain boundary blocks, but the engine treats any non-empty filter workplace as a custom sub-flow. The boundary-only exception currently applies only to the Splitter: `packages/engine/src/executor.ts:123`. Registering a filter implementation alone would therefore not fix newly created filters.
- The product documentation currently combines filtering with finding extraction. That conflicts with your requested “output the remaining data without altering it.” I recommend separating these responsibilities.

These are code-inspection findings; I have not run or changed the app.

**Options**

| Approach | How It Works | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Explicit rules** | Filter by metadata, configured fields, dates, markets or clear exclusion rules. | Fast, predictable, easy to explain, runs locally. | Cannot reliably understand nuanced relevance. Keywords can remove useful information accidentally. |
| **2. Structured LLM classifier** | Give the model criteria and items; require `keep`, `exclude` or `review`, with a reason and supporting quote for each ID. | Flexible prompts; understands context, mixed topics and multilingual feedback. Simplest useful AI implementation. | Cost and latency; decisions can vary. Model-reported confidence is not automatically calibrated. |
| **3. Vector comparison** | Embed each item and compare it with user-approved relevant and irrelevant examples. | Efficient for large datasets; shows similar examples; embeddings can be cached. | Similarity is not relevance. Negation, numbers and mixed-topic comments are difficult. Similarity scores are not probabilities. |
| **4. Jev decision model** | Ask typed questions such as “Does this item contain information relevant to the stated scope?” and apply a documented decision policy. | Fits the existing `DecisionClient` integration; gives structured decision scores. | The current Jev adapter returns decisions and scores, not textual explanations.
